Text | S.Li

Editors | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

This year has been incredibly busy, but I’ve finally found a moment to continue the series on active noise cancellation (ANC)!

The first four parts covered more or less all the basics of ANC headphones. This time I want to talk about something I consider very important in practice: constraining the amplitude of the output signal.

When simulating ANC, we usually ignore hardware parameters such as the maximum output and input voltage of the headphone driver. In real products, though, they matter a great deal. Every ANC system has a linear operating range; beyond it, distortion and other nonlinear effects set in and performance degrades. An adaptive ANC system may even fail to converge. This operating range depends on the hardware performance of the headphone driver itself (including the sound card).

Back to first principles: active noise cancellation means using the headphone driver to play back sound of the same magnitude as the noise you hear, but in antiphase. A driver’s output can’t be infinitely large, though. If the noise source were a huge explosion, do you think a headphone driver could play back sound just as loud to cancel it? Obviously not.

Within the normal volume range, headphones behave linearly; beyond it, distortion and nonlinearity appear. Why? I’ve drawn a simple figure to illustrate.

Figure 1: Amplitude constraint on the output signal in the time domain (left: original signal; right: signal after clipping)

In Figure 1, the x-axis is time and the y-axis is signal amplitude. Suppose the blue curve on the left is the ideal output signal and the red lines mark the maximum amplitude the driver can output. Clearly the sine wave’s peaks exceed the driver’s normal operating range and will be ruthlessly clipped. The signal actually output after clipping is shown on the right. As you can see, it is no longer a sine wave but something closer to a rectangular wave. In the frequency domain, this distorted signal is no longer narrowband: other frequencies appear. This is a nonlinear effect. Because the signal on the right is no longer the one we wanted in the first place, ANC performance suffers. So how can we constrain the amplitude of the output signal while keeping distortion and nonlinearity down?

This article focuses on amplitude-constraint methods for adaptive feedforward filters [1]. Figure 2 shows the feedforward noise-cancelling system based on an FxLMS adaptive filter that I discussed before. I hope you still remember what the symbols mean. I won’t go over them again here; if you’ve forgotten, take a look at the earlier article Everything you wanted to know about noise-cancelling headphones, part 2: adaptive feedforward ANC.

Figure 2: Rough block diagram of FxLMS adaptive feedforward ANC

Let’s recall the update equation of the FxLMS-based feedforward ANC filter [2]:

𝐰(n+1)=𝐰(n)+μ𝐱′(n)e(n) (1)

where 𝐰(n) are the filter coefficients at time n, μ is the step size, e(n) is the residual noise at time n (measured by the error mic), and 𝐱′(n) is the input signal filtered by the (estimated) secondary path 𝐆′(z). Building on the FxLMS update, there are broadly two ways to constrain the output signal.

The first is called leaky FxLMS. Skipping the long-winded derivation, here is the key update equation:

𝐰(k+1)=(1−μγ)𝐰(k)+μ𝐱′(k)e(k) (2)

Compared with the FxLMS update, this equation introduces a coefficient γ to limit the output. When γ=0, it reduces to the ordinary FxLMS update. The value of γ has to be tuned to the output threshold and the step size.

The second method is to change the direction of adaptation. It is still based on FxLMS, just with an extra condition. When the output is below a threshold C, the update is the same as equation (1). When the output exceeds C, however, the output and the filter coefficients are rescaled. In other words, the direction of adaptation changes:

If |y(n)|=|𝐰T(n)𝐱(n)|≤C,

then 𝐰(n+1)=𝐰(n)+μ𝐱′(n)e(n);

otherwise, if |y(n)|=|𝐰T(n)𝐱(n)|>C,

then

1: 𝐰(n+1)=𝐰(n+1)[C/|y(n+1)|]

2: y(n+1)=y(n+1)[C/|y(n+1)|].

This keeps the output amplitude within ±C. The filter coefficients are rescaled according to the rated output threshold and the current output amplitude, which changes the direction of adaptation. Compared with the standard FxLMS algorithm, this one needs more multiplications and divisions, and therefore more computing power.

Shi et al. [1] proposed an optimized method for constraining the output. It, too, works by changing the direction of adaptation. Its update equations are derived from the average power of the output. I won’t take the time to walk through the derivation here (see [1] for the details) and will go straight to the key equations:

If |y(n)|=|𝐰T(n)𝐱(n)|≤C,

then 𝐰(n+1)=𝐰(n)+μ𝐱′(n)e(n);

otherwise, if |y(n)|=|𝐰T(n)𝐱(n)|>C,

then

𝐰(n+1)=𝐰(n)−μy(n)𝐱(n).

Note also that when |y(n)|>C, changing the direction of adaptation does not guarantee that the instantaneous amplitude will drop below the threshold right away, so an additional safeguard is needed:

if y(n)>C, then y(n)=C;

otherwise, if y(n)<−C, then y(n)=−C.

This ensures that the instantaneous output amplitude always stays within the linear operating range. The method was proposed in [1] and named the two-gradient direction FXLMS (2GD-FXLMS) algorithm.

I haven’t tried these methods myself yet and am looking forward to experimenting with them when I have time. Personally, I have used an approach similar to audio compression (dynamic range compression, DRC) to constrain the amplitude, and it worked well and is quite practical. Anyone who works in audio will know DRC. While the input signal stays below a set threshold, the output follows it 1:1. Once the input exceeds the threshold, the output no longer follows 1:1 but is reduced by a set ratio, so that the final output never exceeds the maximum output amplitude.

The nonlinearity caused by distortion can of course also be tackled with nonlinear ANC algorithms, such as the methods reviewed in [3]. But nonlinear ANC is computationally very demanding and hard to run effectively in real time.

The main purpose of this article is to remind everyone working on ANC headphones that ANC depends not only on algorithms but also on the hardware parameters of the headphone driver. The methods described here only reduce distortion and nonlinearity; they cannot eliminate them. And of course, if the driver has a wide linear operating range, designing the ANC system becomes far easier.

Questions and corrections are very welcome

Author: S.Li

PhD in acoustics from Germany, now working in China~ Main research topics include stereo, binaural audio, psychoacoustics and active noise cancellation. Always happy to hang out and talk shop with anyone working on similar topics ^_^

References:

[1] Shi, D. Y., Gan, W.‑S., Lam, B., and Shi, C. (2019) “Two‑gradient direction FXLMS: an adaptive active noise control algorithm with output constraint.” Mechanical Systems and Signal Processing, 116, 651‑667. doi:10.1016/j.ymssp.2018.06.062.

[2] Y.Kajikawa, W.-S. Gan, and S. M. Kuo. (2012) “Recent advances on active noise control: open issues and innovative applications.” APSIPA Transactions on Signal and Information Processing 1.

[3] N. V. George, G. Panda (2013) “Advances in active noise control: A survey, with emphasis on recent nonlinear techniques,” Signal Processing. 93 363–377. 12 doi:10.1016/j.sigpro.2012.08.013.
